problem: Source states the condition as fact ("When the principle of equality is in growth ... as is now the case in Europe"); candidate adds a hedge ("may be growing"). Also "pushes their inhabitants together" adds a sense of joining that the source lacks.
replacement: When the principle of equality is growing not only within a single nation but across several neighboring nations at the same time, as is now the case in Europe, the inhabitants of these countries come to resemble one another in their shared dread of war and their common love of peace, however different their languages, customs and laws. *a Ambition or anger may put weapons in the hands of princes, but to no purpose: a general apathy and goodwill calms them in spite of themselves, the sword drops from their grasp, and wars become rarer. The spread of equality in several countries at once also impels their various inhabitants alike toward manufacturing and commerce. Their tastes then grow alike, and their interests become so mixed and entangled that no nation can do harm to others without the harm coming back on itself. In the end all nations see war as a calamity, almost as severe for the conqueror as for the conquered. So in democratic ages it is extremely difficult, on the one hand, to draw nations into hostilities; on the other hand, it is almost impossible for any two of them to go to war without involving the rest. The interests of all are so interlaced, and their opinions and needs so much alike, that none can stay quiet when the others are stirring. Wars therefore become rarer, but when they do break out they spread over a wider field. Neighboring democratic nations not only become alike in some respects; they end up resembling each other in almost all. *b This likeness between nations has very important consequences for war.

problem: "ought of course to strive" sharpened to "must of course strive".
replacement: Suppose I ask why the Helvetic Confederacy made the greatest and most powerful nations of Europe tremble in the fifteenth century, while today that country’s power is exactly proportioned to its population. I see that the Swiss have become like all the surrounding communities, and those surrounding communities like the Swiss. Since numerical strength is now the only difference between them, victory necessarily goes to the largest army. One consequence of the democratic revolution going on in Europe, then, is to make numerical strength prevail on every battlefield and to force all small nations either to merge with large States or at least to adopt their policy. Because numbers decide victory, every people ought of course to strive by every means in its power to put the greatest possible number of men in the field. When it was possible to recruit a kind of troops superior to all others, such as the Swiss infantry or the French cavalry of the sixteenth century, it was not thought necessary to raise very large armies. But matters change when one soldier is as good as another.

problem: Dropped "suddenly" in "no other resource than suddenly to seize upon the whole engine of government"; the point is the sudden stroke versus a war.
replacement: I will add only a few words on civil wars, for fear of exhausting the reader’s patience. Most of what I have said about foreign wars applies a fortiori to civil wars. Men who live in democracies are not naturally inclined to the military character. They sometimes take it on when they have been dragged into the field by compulsion. But rising in a body and voluntarily exposing themselves to the horrors of war, and especially civil war, is a course that the men of democracies are not apt to take. Only the most adventurous members of the community agree to run such risks; the bulk of the population stays motionless. Even if the population were inclined to act, considerable obstacles would stand in its way. It has no old, well-established influence that it is willing to obey, no well-known leaders to rally the discontented as well as to discipline and lead them, and no political powers subordinate to the supreme power of the nation that could give effective support to resistance directed against the government. In democratic countries the moral power of the majority is immense, and the physical resources at its command are out of all proportion to those that could be combined against it. Therefore the party that occupies the seat of the majority, speaks in its name and wields its power, triumphs instantly and irresistibly over all private resistance. It does not even give such opposition time to exist but nips it in the bud. Those who seek to bring about a revolution by force of arms in such nations have no other resource than suddenly to seize the whole machinery of government as it stands, and a single blow can do that better than a war. For as soon as a regular war begins, the party that represents the state is always certain to win. The only case in which a civil war could arise is if the army split into two factions, one raising the standard of rebellion and the other remaining loyal. An army is a small community, very closely united, endowed with great vitality, and able to supply its own needs for some time. Such a war might be bloody, but it could not be long. Either the rebellious army would win over the government by the mere display of its resources, or by its first victory, and then the war would be over; or the struggle would take place, and then the part of the army not supported by the organized powers of the state would quickly either disband or be destroyed. It may therefore be accepted as a general truth that in ages of equality civil wars will become much less frequent and shorter. *c

problem: "ready to admit that it has the right to do whatever it pleases" became "concede that it may do whatever it likes", which reads as possibility rather than right.
replacement: Look closely at our contemporaries and dig down to the roots of their political opinions, and you will meet some of the ideas I have just described. The agreement may even come as a surprise, among men who so often disagree. Americans hold that in every State the supreme power ought to come from the people. Once that power exists, however, they can imagine hardly any limit to it, and they are ready to concede that it has the right to do whatever it likes. They have not the faintest notion of special privileges for cities, families or persons. It seems never to have occurred to them that the same laws might fail to be applied, with strict uniformity, to every part and every inhabitant. These same opinions are spreading further in Europe. They are even working their way into the nations that most vehemently reject the sovereignty of the people. Those nations trace the supreme power to a different source but attribute the same characteristics to it. In all of them the idea of intermediate powers is growing faint and being erased. The idea of rights belonging inherently to certain individuals is fast vanishing from men’s minds, and the idea that society at large is omnipotent and sole authority is rising to fill the space. As social conditions grow more equal and men more alike, these ideas take root and spread. Equality produces them, and they in turn speed equality along.

problem: Hedge added: source says the unity, ubiquity and omnipotence of power constitute the principal characteristics of ALL political systems put forward in our age; candidate says they mark "nearly every" system.
replacement: In France, the revolution I am discussing has gone further than anywhere else in Europe, and these opinions there have taken full possession of the public mind. Listen carefully to what the various French parties say, and you will find that every one has adopted them. Most of the parties condemn the government’s conduct, but all of them believe it should act without pause and meddle in everything that is done. Even the parties most opposed to each other agree on this. The unity, ubiquity and omnipotence of the supreme power, together with the uniformity of its rules, are the principal characteristics of all the political systems put forward in our age. They turn up even in the wildest visions of political regeneration, and the human mind chases them in its dreams. If private individuals come to these ideas spontaneously, princes feel their pull still more strongly. The ancient fabric of European society is being altered and dissolved. Sovereigns are forming new conceptions of what they can do and what they owe. They are learning, for the first time, that the central power they stand for may and should administer all the affairs of the whole community through its own agents, on a single plan. I will venture to say that no monarch in Europe had conceived this opinion before our time. It now sinks deep into the minds of kings and remains there amid every stirring of more restless thought.

problem: Conditional "If it be true that ... men readily adopt" turned into a flat assertion, and "it cannot be doubted" weakened/changed to "just as certain".
replacement: If it is true that men in ages of equality readily take up the idea of a great central power, it cannot be doubted, on the other hand, that their habits and feelings dispose them to accept such a power and back it. A few words will show this, since I have already given most of the reasons. *a People in democratic countries have no superiors, no inferiors and no habitual or necessary partners in what they undertake. They easily turn in on themselves and think of themselves as separate beings. I made this point at some length when I dealt with individualism. As a result, it always takes an effort for such men to pull themselves away from their private affairs and attend to public business. Their natural leaning is to hand that business over to the one visible, lasting representative of the community’s interests, namely the state. They do not merely lack a taste for public business; they frequently lack the time. Private life in democratic periods is so busy, so feverish, so crowded with desires and labors, that each individual has almost no energy or leisure left for public life. I would be the last to claim that these inclinations cannot be overcome, since my main purpose in writing this book has been to fight them. My claim is only that today a hidden force is nourishing them in the human heart, and that unless they are checked they will smother it completely.

problem: "in proportion as all other passions droop and die" became "while every other passion droops", losing the proportional relation.
replacement: I have also had occasion to show that two things make democratic nations dread any violent disturbance: the growing love of well-being and the shifting nature of property. Often the love of public tranquility is the only passion such nations still have, and it grows more active and powerful in them in proportion as every other passion droops and dies. This naturally leads the members of the community to keep handing over further rights to the central power, or giving them up. That power alone seems to have a stake in defending those rights, and to use the same means for them that it uses for itself. In ages of equality, nobody is obliged to help his fellow men, and nobody has any right to expect much support from them. Everyone is therefore independent and powerless at once. These two conditions must never be looked at separately or run together, for they give the citizen of a democratic country quite opposite inclinations. His independence fills him with self-reliance and pride among his equals. His weakness makes him feel, now and then, that he needs help from outside. He cannot hope for it from any of them, since they are all powerless and unsympathetic. In this plight he naturally looks to the imposing power that alone stands above the general level of depression. His needs, and above all his desires, keep calling that power to his mind, until in the end he sees it as the only support his weakness can have, and a necessary one. *b This may go further toward explaining a common sight in democratic countries. The very men who cannot bear superiors will put up patiently with a master, and so show their pride and their servility together.
